title: Antigen-specific T cells in immunotherapy-associated acute kidney injury
text:
Immunotherapy has become a standard therapy for many cancers, but it is associated with a risk of acute
kidney injury, resulting in significantly increased mortality. Overall goal of this study is to delineate the roles of
antigen-specific T cells in immunotherapy-associated acute kidney injury, using novel animal models. The
study will lead to better understanding of the mechanisms of immunotherapy-associated kidney injury and
identification of potential therapeutic targets.

title: Investigating the role of protein quality control in osmotic stress adaptation
text:
Hypertonic exposure causes cell shrinkage and is thought to induce in vivo protein misfolding and aggregation,
which are hallmarks for aging, cancer, and neurodegeneration. However, no studies have determined which
endogenous proteins are compromised by hypertonicity, and little is known about the mechanisms that
maintain proteome integrity during osmotic stress. The experiments proposed here will characterize the protein
quality consequences and responses to hypertonic exposure, identifying determining factors for protein
aggregation, refolding, and degradation that may inspire therapeutic strategies for protein-misfolding diseases.

title: Cancer Biology Program
text: The Cancer Biology (CB) Program is a new program established in 2021, in part through the merger of components of the previous Tumor Biology and Cancer Genetics and Genomics Programs. The CB program serves as the epicenter of basic cancer research at the Duke Cancer Institute. The 58 full members of the CB program integrate strengths in basic science across 16 departments and 4 schools within Duke University. These include genetic and tissue engineering, bioinformatics and computational biology, developmental cell biology, virology and innate immunology, metabolism, biochemistry, cell signaling, DNA replication, repair, and transcriptional and post-transcriptional gene regulation. The multi-disciplinary CB program aims to provide a mechanistic understanding of the entire cancer continuum encompassing tumor initiation, progression, metastasis, and emergence of therapy resistance. The long-term goal of the CB program is to provide support to the faculty and trainees across the basic sciences enabling innovative, high-impact collaborative cancer research. To achieve this goal, we focus on three specific aims: 1) Characterize the underlying molecular genetic processes that promote carcinogenesis; 2) Define the mechanisms in cellular signaling and metabolism that promote tumor development, recurrence, and metastasis; 3) Train the next generation of cancer researchers. To achieve the goals of the third aim, we have developed a robust program of mentoring activities and career development workshops for CB trainees in partnership with the DCI CRTEC. The CB program is home to two T32 programs, the Viral Oncology Training Program and the Pharmacology Scientist Training Program. CB works closely with COE to ensure that our research is relevant to the DCI catchment area priorities and participating in bi-directional communications with our catchment area community. Accomplishments over this grant period include: 1) Recruitment of leading cancer biologists Trudy Oliver, PhD and Greg Wang, PhD to Duke University in the areas of tumor cell plasticity, metabolism and epigenetics; 2) Successfully competing for new collaborative awards including a U01 award on the role of EBV and tumor cell heterogeneity in non-Hodgkin Lymphomas, a DOD partnering PI award on breast cancer brain metastasis, a P01 on molecular alterations contributing to CCM pathogenesis, and U54 award on fusion proteins in rhabdomyosarcoma; 3) Generating a new mechanism to increase recruitment of junior faculty through the creation of the Duke Next Generation Leaders by CB program members. Total direct funding for primary program members is $19M, of which $17.9M is peer-reviewed, including $6.3 M from the NCI. Since the inception of the program in 2021 through 2023, program members published 337 cancer-focused papers, 45 (13%) are intra-programmatic, 112 (33%) are inter-programmatic collaborations and 117 (35%) are in journals with impact factor over 10.

title: Synthetic Multivalent Galectin Assemblies as Anti-Inflammatory Therapies
text:
Harnessing the activity of natural immunoregulatory molecules to treat chronic inflammation is an attractive
strategy to address the limited effectiveness and deleterious side-effects of conventional anti-inflammatory
drugs. The proposed research will develop a new anti-inflammatory therapy based on synthetic multivalent
nanoassemblies of galectin-1 and galectin-3, carbohydrate-binding proteins that are natural regulators of
inflammation. Combining galectin-1 and galectin-3 into a synthetic nanoassembly will address the biochemical
features of wild-type galectins that have limited their therapeutic effectiveness to date, thereby leading to a potent
new class of anti-inflammatory therapy.

title: Unraveling Neural Diversity: Decoding the Cellular and Molecular Mechanisms of Neural Circuit Formation and Function in the Drosophila Central Complex
text:
Proper brain function depends on the precise number and type of neurons formed during development,
with disturbances in genetic programs leading to severe neurological disorders. Our proposal uses
Drosophila neural stem cells that are similar to human outer radial glia to unravel the mechanisms
regulating neural diversity while training diverse next-generation neuroscientists. Given the high
conservation of neural stem cells, genes, and behaviors we study, our work will provide novel insights into
human brain development and disorders and advance our ability to harness stem cells to replace cells lost
to injury or disease.

title: Cancer Prevention And Control Training Grant (CAPACITY)
text:
The prevention of cancer and the delivery of high quality, innovative care to cancer patients are high
priorities for researchers, clinicians, and the general public. The overall goal of the CAPACiTy post-doctoral
training grant is to provide a comprehensive career development training program for PhD/MD trainees in
the skills and competencies needed to conduct rigorous research in cancer control and translational
science. Upon completion of training, early stage investigators will be able to lead and collaborate on high
impact, cancer control research.

title: Regulated and evolutionary responses to nutritional stress
text:
My lab has pioneered work defining the regulation of cell quiescence and elucidating the role of copy number
variation in adaptive evolutions. We aim to extend these advances by studying i) remodeling of gene
expression and cell biology in quiescent cells and ii) the dynamics and functional effects of copy number
variation. These studies build on our prior work and will contribute to our understanding of cell quiescence and
copy number variation in the context of human health and disease.

title: STAT3 variants as a rheostat of immune tolerance
text:
(Overall)
This is a program project grant that is centered on improving our understanding of how immune dysregulation
can arise and lead to autoimmunity and inflammation. The results of the projects here will help improve our
ability to both detect and devise logical treatment strategies for autoimmunity and immune dysregulation.

title: Human endothelial cell regulation of ossification
text:
Bone grafting remains the preferred treatment for bone defects, but this practice is limited by donor site morbidity.
Alternatively, we seek to develop therapies that exploit the bone-regenerating potential of a specific type of bone
marrow-derived stem cells. Here, we propose studies to understand how blood vessels regulate these human
stem cells' activity, paving the way to more rational therapeutic strategies in the regeneration of bone defects.

title: The Central Biochemistry Laboratory for the Chronic Kidney Disease in Children Cohort (CKiD)
text:
This project is relevant to public health as kidney disease is a major cost and national health concern. By
monitoring chronic kidney disease (CKD) with laboratory diagnostic measurements in pediatrics to adults, it
provides an opportunity for insight into underlying disease mechanisms and their relation to cardiovascular risk,
social/behavioral development, and CKD progression. To accomplish the above we will be providing
laboratory services ranging from routine laboratory diagnostics, gold standard measured glomerular filtration
rate testing, novel biomarker analysis, and overall support of the specimens collected for the CKiD study.

title: The role of tumor cell-of-origin-specific PDL1 on tumorigenesis and tumor progression
text:
Here we study tumor-intrinsic PDL1 signals in early carcinogenesis and progression using a novel autochthonous
murine model in which mice develop NrasQ61R-mutant melanomas accelerated by UV exposure that lack PDL1
in the tumor cell-of-origin from initiation, definitively distinguishing biologic PDL1 signals versus compensatory
mechanisms that could confound prior genetic PDL1KO studies. Our work defining tumor-intrinsic PDL1 signals
in early carcinogenesis and their contribution to tumor progression and the tumor microenvironment provides
insights into novel targetable ways in which PDL1 suppresses antitumor immunity. Our data can help improve
melanoma treatments or response biomarkers.

title: Molecular and Cell Biology Core (MCBC)
text: The Molecular and Cell Biology Core (MCBC) of the Center for Lung Biology and Disease (CLBD) has been created to meet the need for advanced molecular biology support by PJIs. The current application includes four more JPI-led full projects that hold exceptional promise for being developed as independent investigators who can compete nationally for categorial NIH funding. These projects require advanced molecular and cellular biological principles, methods, and advances in genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, immunology, and microscopy to delineate fundamental cellular mechanisms leading to disease outcomes. In this Phase II renewal application, the Molecular and Cell Biology Core (MCBC) proposes to continue to leverage, coordinate, and expand the resources and expertise of the Division of Biotechnology and Molecular Medicine (BIOMMED) at the LSU School of Veterinary Medicine. BIOMMED administers and coordinates access to specialized Core Facilities, including the Gene Expression and Sequencing Laboratory (GeneLab), Viral Vectors Laboratory, Protein Characterization and Purification Laboratory, which also generates monospecific and monoclonal antibodies, and coordinates and facilitates access to a variety of other LSU Vet Med resources including the LSU Vet Med Microscopy Center and the Shared Instrumentation Facility (main campus) which provides advanced immunofluorescence and electron microscopy. MCBC offers biostatistics and advanced bioinformatics analyses to analyze complex genomic and transcriptomic data to LSU and Louisiana researchers in close collaboration with the LSU Center for Computation & Technology. MCBC aims to provide and coordinate access to advanced instrumentation and services and develop and offer new molecular methodologies. MCBC will also provide training for molecular biology and cell biology methodologies to all PJIs and other NIH-funded investigators to achieve their research objectives. The MCBC has two specific aims: Aim 1. To provide the Center and other NIH-funded investigators with resources and expertise on advanced molecular biology technologies, instrumentation, technical support, and development of molecular assays needed for their projects. Aim 2. To organize, coordinate, and facilitate interactions among COBRE investigators, mentors, and students; train PJIs and other faculty, staff, and students in advanced molecular biology technologies; and establish long-term sustainability of all core services and functions. The MCBC centralized molecular and cell biology services and training will provide outstanding capabilities in molecular and cell biology methodologies. MCBC will streamline experimental tasks to maximize efficiency, productivity, benefits, and efficient use of reagents, as well as assist PJIs in adopting and developing new technological molecular and cell biology approaches.

title: Escape from CAR T surveillance through lineage plasticity
text:
Despite the effectiveness of CAR T therapy for patients with refractory B cell
malignancies, approximately 50% of patients relapse within one year of treatment. A
common cause of relapse is the emergence of CAR-resistant leukemias. Our proposal
develops two key models for studying mechanisms of relapse following cellular therapy
for leukemia and identifies avenues for improving durability of remission.

title: Interdisciplinary Research Training Center in Cancer Care Delivery
text: The delivery of cancer care is complex and expensive and is often of suboptimal quality. This interdisciplinary training program for pre and postdoctoral trainees focuses on preparing scientists to become independent investigators to conduct cancer care delivery research that will ultimately improve the care experience for patients with cancer. With the support of their mentors, formal coursework, selected emphasis activities, and professional socialization, trainees will acquire skills in descriptive discovery research, intervention development and testing, and implementation science to address critical gaps in cancer care delivery.

title: Project 3: InHANCE: Fibrosis Imaging Biomarkers of Radiation: An Orphan Drug Study to Evaluate REduction of SeVERity of Symptoms in a Randomized Evaluative Trial (FIBRO2SE-REVERSE)
text:
Project 3
This project addresses the critical challenge of managing post-therapy radiation-induced lymphedema and
fibrosis in head and neck cancer patients, conditions that significantly impact quality of life by leading to
debilitating dysphagia and trismus. It aims to assess the effectiveness of off-label FDA-approved drugs in
reversing late-stage fibrosis through a Phase II pragmatic trial, alongside the development of innovative deep
learning methods to quantify the severity of lymphedema and fibrosis using MRI imaging, in addition to biomarker
validation of MRI relaxometry for monitoring radiation-induced swallowing muscle fibrosis.

title: Impact of Epidemiologically Based Phthalate Exposures on Female Reproduction and Metabolism
text:
Female metabolic and reproductive disease are a worldwide concern and exposure to phthalates is thought to
contribute to their incidence. This work is aimed at identifying the target tissues and processes related to
metabolism and reproduction that affected by phthalates in females. Results from these experiments will
enhance our understanding of the risks posed by phthalates and contribute to the development of screening
tools and therapeutic strategies to detect and treat phthalate-induced metabolic and reproductive disorders.

title: Cell-type specific control of alcohol-associated behavior in the striatum
text:
Cues associated with the availability of alcohol can trigger seeking, increase drinking behavior, and contribute
to relapse in alcohol use disorder, suggesting a critical need to understand the neural mechanisms encoding
this information and how they change with long-term drinking and abstinence. This proposal aims to
understand how neural circuits encode information about alcohol-associated cues in vivo and how chronic
alcohol exposure impacts these circuits to drive alcohol seeking.

title: Integrated multimodal phenotyping of zebrafish models of human cognitive disorders
text:
New research methods have made it possible to create and characterize dozens of animal models of human
cognitive disorders in parallel. By combining high throughput CRISPR technology with state-of-the-art
sequencing, imaging, and behavioral assays, this project will generate highly detailed quantitative descriptions
of dozens of distinct models of human neurodevelopmental disorders in zebrafish. Computational tools will then
be used to interpret, relate, and predict phenotypes, providing insights about the cellular and molecular pathways
involved in brain development and cognitive dysfunction.

title: Establishing Force-Based Metrics and Haptic Feedback to Standardize Robotic Paraesophageal Hernia Repair
text:
Robotic surgery offers many benefits, but a major drawback has been the lack of force feedback, which can lead
to injuries and poor outcomes, especially in complex operations like paraesophageal hernia repairs. This project
will develop new tools that give surgeons real-time feedback on how much force they are using, helping them
perform safer and more effective surgeries. The results could improve recovery, reduce complications, and
create a new standard for robotic surgery across many specialties.

title: Targeting SHP-1 through a newfound metabolite-regulated cysteine activation site
text:
Inhibition of macrophages is an essential step in resolving acute inflammation. A cellular metabolite known as
itaconate was shown to be the major inhibitor of macrophage activation but the exact mechanism by which
itaconate exerts this function remains unclear. Here, we will test if a newfound target of itaconate, a protein
called SHP-1, is responsible for itaconate inhibition of macrophage activity.
